{"status":"ok","message-type":"work-list","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"facets":{},"total-results":1071599,"items":[{"DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.4633965","title":["Combating Alert Fatigue in the Security Operations Centre"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2023]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>It is generally recognised that the demand for experienced cybersecurity professionals outstrips supply by a considerable margin. In consequence, those who are in post are often overworked and under stress. One symptom of this that arises in the Security Operations Centre (SOC) context goes by the name of ‘alert fatigue’ — the SOC analyst is effectively blinded by the sheer volume of system-generated messages demanding attention, most of which turn out not to have security significance. This paper reports on work carried out within the AISOC (AI Security Operations Centre) project, a collaboration between Birmingham City University (BCU) and METCLOUD, a managed service provider. The aim of AISOC is to use Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data Science (DS) techniques to create an intelligent assistant that will reduce the workload and amplify the skills of analysts working in SOCs, resulting in more efficient and effective detection of, response to, and remediation of cyber-attacks. In the process it will increase job satisfaction and staff retention, and enable a more scalable business model. The research contribution presented is a novel approach, named CHILL (Continuous Human-in-the-Loop Learning) whereby human expert and AI agent work as a team, with knowledge being transferred from expert to AI apprentice over time. It also emphasises the ability to interpret observed phenomena in terms of root causes. An early implementation of AISOC is currently being used by METCLOUD analysts on a trial basis alongside their current software tools. Feedback so far validates the concept of an intelligent assistant to reduce workload and to allow more time to be spent on problematic cases of potentially high security significance. The research was informed by a ‘deep dive’ analysis of real alert data generated from events produced by the Windows audit system. This identified two measures we estimate will reduce the number of Windows logon alerts processed by analysts by nearly 90%.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.6703558","title":["Cognitive Alert Triage: A Fuzzy-Logic SOAR Framework for Reducing Analyst Fatigue in Mid-Market Security Operations"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Security Operations Centers face an escalating operational crisis: the volume of alerts generated by modern detection infrastructure consistently exceeds the cognitive capacity of human analysts, producing alert fatigue that degrades detection reliability and accelerates analyst attrition. This problem bears disproportionately on mid-market organizations-those lacking the headcount and infrastructure budget to sustain dedicated 24/7 SOC coverageleaving a substantial fraction of critical infrastructure sectors chronically under-protected. Existing mitigation approaches, including rule-based SOAR automation and threshold-tuned SIEM filtering, address symptoms rather than the structural cause: the absence of an intelligent, adaptive triage layer that can stratify alert populations by behavioral evidence without requiring prior knowledge of attack signatures or continuous playbook engineering. This paper presents the Cognitive Alert Triage (CAT) framework, a fuzzy-logic Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response architecture that automates the alert prioritization layer through a four-stage pipeline: behavioral clustering of SIEM telemetry via DE_Clust_Hell-a Differential Evolution optimizer with Hellinger distance substituting Euclidean fitness, previously validated for noise-robust data classification-followed by fuzzy membership scoring, composite triage queue construction, and threshold-governed automated response dispatch. The framework requires no pre-authored playbooks and adapts to the operational baseline of each deployment through learned behavioral archetypes. Simulation on a CICIDS2017-consistent benchmark dataset under 20% Gaussian noise demonstrates that the Hellinger clustering layer reduces misclassification error by 74.9% relative to a Euclidean baseline (8.67% vs. 34.57%), with ARI improving from 0.420 to 0.801. Applied to a 1,880record dataset containing 680 attack records, the full CAT pipeline achieves a 55% reduction in analyst queue volume while retaining 86.8% attack visibility. The automated escalation band achieves a 100% attack precision rate, eliminating false positives at the highest-priority tier of the analyst workflow. The framework's cloud-native architecture enables a fractional SOC deployment model in which a single platform serves multiple mid-market organizations simultaneously, making continuous intelligent monitoring economically accessible to organizations historically priced out of enterprise-grade cyber defense.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.36227/techrxiv.176765375.53124342/v1","title":["Reducing Alert Fatigue in Cloud Operations: A Practitioner's Approach to Scalable SRE Monitoring"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,1,5]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Alert fatigue represents a critical challenge in modern cloud operations, where excessive notifications and false positives undermine incident response effectiveness and team morale. This paper presents a systematic approach to reducing alert fatigue while maintaining operational visibility, drawn from seven years of Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) experience managing production cloud services. We describe a four-step methodology encompassing alert classification, health check implementation, intelligent automation, and enhanced observability. Applied to a multi-cloud environment supporting 40-50 microservices, this approach reduced critical alerts from 8-10 per day to roughly one per week, corresponding to a reduction of more than ninety percent when normalized on a daily equivalent basis, while simultaneously decreasing Mean Time To Resolution (MTTR) by 80% and achieving 99.98% service uptime. The paper contributes practical insights for SRE teams seeking to balance operational visibility with sustainable on-call practices, demonstrating that strategic alert design significantly improves both system reliability and team effectiveness.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1145/3723158","title":["Alert Fatigue in Security Operations Centres: Research Challenges and Opportunities"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2025,4,4]]},"container-title":["ACM Computing Surveys"],"type":"journal-article","abstract":"<jats:p>A security operations centre (SOC) is a facility where teams of security professionals, supported by advanced technologies and processes, work together to monitor, detect, and respond to cybersecurity incidents. With advances in AI technology, most of the SOC functions are increasingly becoming AI-driven. Among these, real-time alert monitoring and triage is particularly important. Recent studies, by both industry and academia, have highlighted the problem of alert fatigue and burnout in SOC. Several solutions have been proposed in the literature and by the industry to address this problem. In this article, we review the existing literature and industry solutions on alert fatigue mitigation through the lenses of automation, augmentation, and human–AI collaboration. Based on the review, we identify four major causes of alert fatigue in SOC. We also examine the shortcomings of existing solutions and propose several potential research directions leveraging AI. By providing a comprehensive analysis of the state-of-the-art approaches and their limitations, this study contributes to the existing literature in an important field of study. We anticipate that it will inspire new research directions for addressing alert fatigue not just in SOCs but across other Command and Control (C2) domains as well.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1109/iciccs67901.2026.11502746","title":["A Semi-Supervised and Evasion-Aware Framework for Reducing Alert Fatigue in Security Operations Centers (SoC)"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,3,16]]},"container-title":["2026 9th International Conference on Intelligent Computing and Control Systems (ICICCS)"],"type":"proceedings-article"},{"DOI":"10.1145/3474718.3474723","title":["Combat Security Alert Fatigue with AI-Assisted Techniques"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2021,8,9]]},"container-title":["Cyber Security Experimentation and Test Workshop"],"type":"proceedings-article"},{"DOI":"10.1007/979-8-8688-1032-9_11","title":["The Alert Fatigue"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2024]]},"container-title":["Enterprise Digital Reliability"],"type":"book-chapter"},{"DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.7467876","title":["Wazuh Alert Manager: An OpenSearch plugin for alert and case management in Wazuh-based Security Operations Centers"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Security analysts using Wazuh for security monitoring typically report experiencing high alert volumes. However, in the Wazuh 4.12-4.14 dashboards considered in this paper, there is no native way to manage the alert lifecycle, analyst workload, handle independent multi-alert cases, or automate alert workflows. As a result, many SOCs running Wazuh add external case management tools like TheHive and DFIR-IRIS, increasing the technology stack and operational complexity. In this paper, we present the Wazuh Alert Manager plugin v2.0.2, built for Wazuh dashboard versions 4.12-4.14, to provide alert and case management, alert workflow automation, and reporting within the Wazuh dashboard. The plugin writes only to its indexes and only performs reads from Wazuh native alert indexes. In three benchmarking tests, the plugin processed 100,000 alerts on a standard all-in-one Wazuh VM with a median time of 238.081 seconds, resulting in exactly 42 cases, 5,000 alert auto-closures, 2,500 auto-assignments, and no actions on 87,200 benign alerts. The plugin is licensed under Apache 2.0 and archived on Zenodo.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1016/j.cose.2023.103583","title":["Combating alert fatigue with AlertPro: Context-aware alert prioritization using reinforcement learning for multi-step attack detection"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2024,2]]},"container-title":["Computers & Security"],"type":"journal-article"},{"DOI":"10.1145/3670009","title":["Towards Human-AI Teaming to Mitigate Alert Fatigue in Security Operations Centres"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2024,7,15]]},"container-title":["ACM Transactions on Internet Technology"],"type":"journal-article","abstract":"<jats:p>
            Security Operations Centres (SOCs) play a pivotal role in defending organisations against evolving cyber threats. They function as central hubs for detecting, analysing, and responding promptly to cyber incidents with the primary objective of ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of digital assets. However, they struggle against the growing problem of alert fatigue, where the sheer volume of alerts overwhelms SOC analysts and raises the risk of overlooking critical threats. In recent times, there has been a growing call for human-AI teaming, wherein humans and AI collaborate with each other, leveraging their complementary strengths and compensating for their weaknesses. The rapid advances in AI and the growing integration of AI-enabled tools and technologies within SOCs give rise to a compelling argument for the implementation of human-AI teaming within the SOC environment. Therefore, in this article, we present our vision for human-AI teaming to address the problem of alert fatigue in the SOC. We propose the 𝒜
            <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
            𝒞 Framework, which enables flexible and dynamic decision making by allowing seamless transitions between automated, augmented, and collaborative modes of operation. Our framework allows AI-powered automation for routine alerts, AI-driven augmentation for expedited expert decision making, and collaborative exploration for tackling complex, novel threats. By implementing and operationalising 𝒜
            <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
            𝒞, SOCs can significantly reduce alert fatigue while empowering analysts to efficiently and effectively respond to security incidents.
          </jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.7163538","title":["Reducing Security Alert Fatigue: A Recommender System for Prioritizing Static Analysis Warnings Based on Historical Developer Feedback"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools are widely adopted in software development pipelines, yet they generate an overwhelming volume of warnings, the majority of which are false positives or low-priority issues. This forces developers to manually triage hundreds of alerts per commit, resulting in alert fatigue and the frequent oversight of genuine vulnerabilities. This paper presents a recommender system that prioritizes SAST warnings using collaborative filtering based on historical developer feedback. We model the triage process as a recommendation problem where repositories serve as users, SAST warnings as items, and implicit ratings are derived from developer actions-fixes indicate actionable warnings, while dismissals or suppressions indicate false positives or accepted risks. Our system leverages a repository of historical triage decisions to predict, for a new warning, the likelihood that developers will consider it actionable. Unlike generic severity scores such as CVSS, our approach incorporates contextual features including programming language, framework versions, dependency graphs, and warning characteristics such as CWE classification and data-flow complexity. We evaluate our system using historical SAST reports and developer remediation data from open-source repositories and enterprise environments. Experimental results demonstrate that our collaborative filtering approach achieves higher precision at top-k rankings than severity-based baselines, reducing manual inspection effort by over 60% without compromising detection of critical vulnerabilities. We further address the cold-start problem through a hybrid strategy that leverages repository similarity. Our work demonstrates that collaborative filtering offers a practical, scalable solution to alert fatigue, improving both developer productivity and security outcomes.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1109/icbats66542.2025.11258356","title":["Machine Learning Solution for Healthcare Efficiency for AI-Based ECG Alert System to Address Alert (ICAIC)"],"type":"proceedings-article"},{"DOI":"10.30574/wjarr.2026.31.3.2442","title":["HUMAN COGNITIVE RESILIENCE IN SECURITY OPERATIONS CENTERS: A STRUCTURED REVIEW AND QUANTITATIVE FRAMEWORK FOR SLEEP, ALERT FATIGUE, WORKLOAD, AND HUMAN-AI CYBER DEFENSE"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,9,30]]},"container-title":["World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews"],"type":"journal-article","abstract":"<jats:p>This review examines how sleep restriction, cumulative fatigue, alert overload, cognitive workload, occupational stress, burnout, and human-AI task allocation shape the cognitive conditions under which Security Operations Center (SOC) analysts and incident responders perform. The review updates and integrates evidence from cybersecurity, cognitive neuroscience, occupational psychology, human factors, and organizational resilience through August 2026. The synthesis distinguishes direct cybersecurity evidence from transferred evidence and identifies a persistent empirical gap: cyber operations clearly exhibit fatigue, workload, burnout, and alert-management pressure, but direct longitudinal evidence connecting objectively measured sleep and cognitive state to operational cyber outcomes remains limited. To move beyond a descriptive human-factors account, we refine the Human Cognitive Resilience Framework (HCRF) as a testable socio-technical model linking operational demands, cognitive load and occupational stress, organizational resources, cognitive resilience, cybersecurity performance, organizational cyber resilience, and organizational learning. The revised framework incorporates 2026 developments in human-centered cybersecurity and human-AI incident management, and introduces a quantitative operationalization for repeated-measures field testing. Recommended measurements combine sleep/actigraphy, psychomotor vigilance, workload and stress instruments, analyst telemetry, objective triage and response metrics, and organizational-resource indicators. Formal mediation, moderation, nonlinear threshold, and multilevel hypotheses are specified. The resulting framework treats human cognitive capacity neither as a substitute for technical controls nor as an individual responsibility problem, but as an operational resource jointly shaped by work design, staffing, recovery, automation, leadership, and team processes.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.22214/ijraset.2025.73727","title":["Enhancing Alert Prioritization in Enterprise Security Operations via Factor Graph Modeling"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2025,8,31]]},"container-title":["International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology"],"type":"journal-article","abstract":"<jats:p>Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain one of the most challenging problems in enterprise cybersecurity due to
their stealthy, multi-stage nature and ability to evade traditional detection methods. While existing systems like RANK utilize
factor graph-based scoring to correlate alerts into actionable incident graphs, they rely on static, manually defined tactic
transition weights, limiting adaptability to emerging attack pat- terns. In this paper, we propose an enhancement to the RANK
architecture by introducing an adaptive scoring mechanism based on pairwise factor graphs. Our approach dynamically models
contextual and temporal relationships between MITRE ATT&CK tactics, enabling more accurate and flexible incident evaluation.
Experiments conducted on two enterprise-scale datasets show that our method improves detection precision and F1 scores while
maintaining compatibility with real-world alert streams. These results demonstrate the potential of adaptive, context- aware
scoring in reducing false positives and enhancing threat detection capabilities in modern Security Operations Centers.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.14722/ndss.2019.23349","title":["NoDoze: Combatting Threat Alert Fatigue with Automated Provenance Triage"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2019]]},"container-title":["Proceedings 2019 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium"],"type":"proceedings-article"},{"DOI":"10.55041/ijsrem61191","title":["MCP-Driven RAG Architecture for Automated Alert Triage in Security Operations Centers"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,4,25]]},"container-title":["INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT"],"type":"journal-article","abstract":"<jats:p>Abstract
Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are the first line of defense against cyber threats, but they are becoming more and more overwhelmed by the large number and complexity of alerts that modern enterprise infrastructure generates. Surveys of the industry show that false-positive rates in enterprise SIEM deployments often go over 60%. This constant noise makes analysts tired, lowers the quality of decisions, and gives attackers chances to work without being seen. Rule-based correlation engines, supervised machine learning classifiers, and SOAR platforms are some of the current solutions. They only solve part of the problem, and they all have a major flaw: they can't automatically add new threat intelligence, and none of them give clear reasons for triage decisions. This paper presents a unified architecture that integrates the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline to facilitate intelligent, explainable, and real-time alert triage in Security Operations Center (SOC) settings. Anthropic released MCP as an open standard in November 2024 [10]. It is a standardized JSON-RPC 2.0 integration layer that links an LLM reasoning engine to CVE databases, the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base, curated incident repositories, and live threat intelligence feeds. RAG gives the model relevant external context at inference time without having to retrain it. The LLM then makes structured triage decisions and gives analysts step-by-step reasoning chains that they can check, change, and learn from.

A proof-of-concept implementation was evaluated using the CICIDS2017 benchmark dataset [7] through a reproducible simulation pipeline that produced a corpus of 47,312 synthetic SIEM alerts. Important Caveat: All performance metrics reported in this paper are from the proof-of-concept implementation within a simulation pipeline running on 2017-era network traffic and are not production performance claims. The 61.4% simulation-generated baseline FPR was generated within the simulation itself and was not validated against an actual SIEM deployment. All reported improvements over baselines should be understood relative to this simulation-generated FPR only. Within these limits, the proposed system achieved a FPR, TPR, and a mean triage latency of 3.91 ± 0.52 seconds. All gains over three baseline configurations are statistically significant (p < 0.001 via two-proportion z-test). The overall score in the explainability assessment from three certified SOC analysts was 4.6/5.0, which is not generalizable outside of this group and should be considered only as an initial indication of explainability until further, larger studies (n >= 30) are completed. Component-level latency is discussed based on profiling and attributed to the use ofMCPresponse caching(meancache-hit rate 62.3%)andstructuredcontext prompt compression.The RAG-only baseline did not utilize equivalent caching, thus partially confounding comparison. Contemporary attack dataset evaluation was prioritized as a target for future work.</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1016/j.ins.2026.124128","title":["Adaptive alert prioritisation in security operations centres via learning to defer with human feedback"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2027,1]]},"container-title":["Information Sciences"],"type":"journal-article"},{"DOI":"10.64240/1a004d9ee5","title":["Reducing Alert Fatigue with Real-Time Cyber Threat Detection Tools"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>How can real-time detection technologies reduce cyber risk without overwhelming security analysts?</jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1007/978-3-031-54129-2_36","title":["On the Use of AutoML for Combating Alert Fatigue in Security Operations Centers"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2024]]},"container-title":["Lecture Notes in Computer Science","Computer Security.
